headline: Massachusetts declares energy emergency and expands winter heating aid
dek: A new state plan creates a one-time heating-oil benefit for middle-income households, increases assistance for low-income residents and temporarily removes selected electric-bill charges.
body: Massachusetts is declaring an energy emergency as heating-oil prices rise sharply ahead of winter, while rolling out a package of temporary assistance and utility-bill changes aimed at households across the income spectrum. Gov. Maura Healey's administration says the plan could deliver nearly $150 million in relief, including expanded heating aid, a three-month pause on one electric-bill charge and a reduction in another energy-related obligation. The announcement came Oct. 5 from the [Massachusetts governor's office](https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-new-winter-energy-bill-relief-for-massachusetts-families).

The most targeted new benefit is for households that heat with #2 home heating oil and earn more than 60% but less than 100% of the state's median income. The administration expects about 50,000 households to qualify for a one-time benefit of up to $680. Applications are scheduled to open in December, and the benefit is expected to remain available through April 30, 2027, or until the funding is exhausted. The [state's eligibility page](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/middle-income-heating-oil-relief) lists income thresholds by household size, so the program's broad description should not be treated as automatic eligibility.

For a family of four, the published range runs from more than $103,050 to less than $171,749 in gross household income for fiscal 2027. That income band is significant because it reaches households that may earn too much for traditional low-income energy assistance but still face a large seasonal bill. The benefit is limited to qualifying heating oil, however; the state page does not describe it as a general cash payment or as assistance for every heating source.

The state is also putting an additional $15 million into the Home Energy Assistance Program, known as HEAP. Massachusetts says the increase will reach about 156,000 low-income households, with oil-heated households receiving a 20% increase in assistance and households that heat with utilities receiving a 15% increase. The assistance period is listed as Nov. 1 through April 30, 2027. Renters and homeowners may apply, including some households whose heat is included in rent, through the state's [home-energy assistance portal](https://www.mass.gov/orgs/home-energy-assistance-programs).

The bill changes are broader but shorter-lived. The administration says it will use $80 million in state funding to remove the Solar Massachusetts Renewable Target, or SMART, charge from residential and commercial electric bills for January through March 2027. It also plans to cut the Alternative Energy Portfolio Standard by 50% this winter, which the state estimates will provide another $20 million in ratepayer relief. Those steps lower charges for the covered period; they do not eliminate the underlying programs or guarantee the same reduction on every customer's bill.

The emergency declaration also activates Massachusetts legal protections against petroleum price gouging. The governor's office said state agencies will monitor, investigate and enforce rules against excessive or misleading prices for petroleum products. That enforcement authority is separate from the heating benefits: it is intended to address improper pricing, while the assistance programs help households pay legitimate costs.

The need is tied to a steep change in the heating-oil market. The state said the average Massachusetts home-heating-oil price reached $6.08 per gallon on Sept. 28, compared with $3.52 a year earlier, a 73% increase. The Boston Globe reported the same figures and described the package as a collection of mostly temporary steps, while [WBUR's coverage](https://www.wbur.org/news) placed the move in the wider debate over some of the nation's highest household energy costs. The comparison is a statewide average, not a quote for every town or supplier, and a household's total winter bill will vary with delivery size, weather, insulation and consumption.

About one in five Massachusetts households relies on heating oil, according to the state, with older homes and rural communities especially represented. That makes the new middle-income benefit relevant beyond the state's lowest-income households, but the plan still leaves practical questions for residents: how quickly local administering agencies can process applications, how long the money lasts and what happens after the temporary bill reductions expire. The administration also announced an Emergency Winter Warmth Fund with an initial $100,000 contribution from Citizens Energy Corporation to support existing low-income aid and the new oil benefit.

For residents, the next step is preparation rather than waiting for a crisis. HEAP applications are already routed through the state program and local agencies, while the new middle-income oil benefit is not expected to accept applications until December. The state's announcement says it has also asked Congress for an additional $3 billion in emergency LIHEAP funding, but that request is not enacted federal money. Massachusetts households will therefore be watching both the state rollout and federal appropriations as the heating season begins.
author: NorthEast News Desk
